notes.definition: Work is done when a force causes an object to move through a distance. The work done equals the force multiplied by the distance moved along the line of action of the force (W = Fs), and it equals the energy transferred.
explanation: When a force makes an object move, the force does work on the object. Pushing a trolley along a corridor, lifting a box onto a shelf and a car's brakes slowing it down are all examples of work being done. Doing work is one way of transferring energy: the work done is equal to the energy transferred. If you push hard against a wall and it does not move, no work is done on the wall, because there is no displacement.

The work done is calculated using W = F s, where W is the work done in joules (J), F is the force in newtons (N) and s is the distance in metres (m). The distance must be the distance moved along the line of action of the force, that is, in the same direction as the force. When lifting an object at a steady speed, the force needed equals its weight and the distance is the vertical height it is raised, even if it is carried up a ramp.

One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre. This means that 1 joule = 1 newton-metre (1 J = 1 N m), so a value such as 250 N m is the same as 250 J. Watch the units given in questions: distances in centimetres must be converted to metres by dividing by 100, and work in kilojoules must be converted to joules by multiplying by 1000.

When work is done, energy is transferred from one store to another. When a person pushes a box across a floor, energy is transferred from the chemical store of the person. When a car brakes, the friction force between the brake pads and the discs does work, transferring energy from the kinetic energy store of the car to the thermal energy store of the brakes, which then heat the surroundings.

Work done against frictional forces causes a rise in the temperature of an object. Rubbing your hands together warms them; a drill bit gets hot when drilling; a meteor glows as it moves through the atmosphere. In each case a force acts while the surfaces move past each other, so work is done, and the energy transferred increases the thermal energy store, raising the temperature.
keyFacts: Work is done when a force causes an object to move through a distance.
Work done = force × distance moved along the line of action of the force: W = Fs.
Work done is measured in joules (J); force in newtons (N); distance in metres (m).
1 joule is the work done when a force of 1 N causes a displacement of 1 m.
Work done against friction causes a rise in the temperature of the object.
No displacement means no work done, however large the force.
Convert cm to m (÷ 100) and kJ to J (× 1000) before using W = Fs.

keyTerms.definition: The energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance; W = Fs.
The unit of work and energy; the work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m.
A unit equal to the joule when used for work done: 1 N m = 1 J.
The distance moved in a particular direction.
The straight line along which a force acts; only distance along this line counts in W = Fs.
A force that opposes motion between surfaces; doing work against it raises the temperature.
The movement of energy from one store to another, for example by a force doing work.

equations.name: Work done
equations.formula: work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action of the force)
equations.units: W in joules (J), F in newtons (N), s in metres (m)

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that holding a heavy object still is doing work on it.
misconceptions.right: In fact no work is done on the object because it does not move; work needs a displacement in the direction of the force.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often use any distance in W = Fs.
misconceptions.right: In fact only the distance moved along the line of action of the force counts, e.g. the vertical height when lifting against gravity.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think newton-metres and joules are different quantities when describing work.
misconceptions.right: In fact for work done, 1 N m = 1 J; they are the same unit.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think energy is 'used up' or destroyed by friction.
misconceptions.right: In fact the work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal energy store, raising the temperature; the energy is dissipated, not destroyed.

realWorld: Car and bicycle brakes rely on friction doing work to transfer kinetic energy to thermal energy; racing car brake discs can glow red hot.
Spacecraft need heat shields because work done against air resistance on re-entry raises their surface temperature enormously.
Engineers calculate the work done by lifts and cranes to choose motors with the right energy and power ratings.
Machinists use coolant on drills and lathes because work done against friction would otherwise overheat the tool.
examTips: W = Fs must be recalled; it is not on the equation sheet.
Check the units before substituting: cm to m (÷ 100), kJ to J (× 1000), g to kg (÷ 1000) for weight.
When describing energy transfers, name both stores (e.g. kinetic store to thermal store) and the process (work done by friction).
If asked why something gets hot when rubbed, say work is done against friction, which increases the thermal energy store and the temperature.
Remember that 'newton-metre' and 'joule' are interchangeable for work done; you may be asked to convert.
summary: Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance.
W = F s, with W in J, F in N and s in m.
Work done against friction raises the temperature of the object.
Only distance along the line of action of the force counts.

questions.question: Which equation is used to calculate work done?
questions.explanation: Work done = force × distance moved along the line of action of the force. W = mg is the weight equation.

questions.question: What is the unit of work done?
questions.explanation: Work done is energy transferred, so it is measured in joules. Watts measure power and N/m is the unit of spring constant.

questions.question: Which of these is equal to 1 joule?
questions.explanation: One joule is the work done when 1 N moves an object 1 m, so 1 J = 1 N m.

questions.question:
A wooden block is pushed along a rough bench.
What effect does the work done against friction have on the block?
questions.explanation: Work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal energy store, so the temperature of the block (and bench) rises.

questions.question: In which situation is no work done on the object?
options: A man lifts a suitcase onto a rack
A horse pulls a cart along a road
A student pushes hard against a wall that does not move
A car's brakes slow it down
markScheme: 1 mark: A student pushes hard against a wall that does not move
questions.explanation: Work needs the force to cause a displacement. The wall does not move, so no work is done on it, however hard the student pushes.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a box being pushed along the floor.
A force of 20 N moves the box 3 m in the direction of the force.
How much work is done on the box?
questions.explanation: W = F s = 20 × 3 = 60 J. Dividing or adding the values gives the other answers.

questions.question:
The force pushing a trolley is doubled. The trolley is pushed the same distance.
What happens to the work done?
questions.explanation: W = F s. With s unchanged, work done is directly proportional to force, so it doubles.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a box being pushed at a steady speed up a ramp onto a platform.
The weight of the box is 100 N.
How much work is done against gravity? Ignore friction.
questions.explanation: Work done against gravity uses the distance along the line of action of the weight, which is vertical: 100 × 2 = 200 J. The 5 m ramp length is not in the direction of the weight.

questions.question: A car brakes and stops. Which describes the main energy transfer?
options: Thermal energy store of brakes → kinetic energy store of car
Chemical energy store of fuel → kinetic energy store of car
Kinetic energy store of car → gravitational potential energy store
Kinetic energy store of car → thermal energy store of brakes and surroundings
markScheme: 1 mark: Kinetic energy store of car → thermal energy store of brakes and surroundings
questions.explanation: Friction in the brakes does work on the car, transferring energy from its kinetic store to the thermal store of the brakes, which then heat the surroundings.

questions.question:
A force does 75 N m of work.
What is this work in joules?
questions.explanation: 1 N m = 1 J, so 75 N m = 75 J. No conversion factor is needed.

questions.question:
The equation for work done is W = F s
In which unit must the distance be to give the work done in joules?
questions.explanation: With force in newtons and distance in metres, work done is in joules. Other distance units must be converted to metres first.

questions.question:
A force of 20 N pushes a trolley a distance of 5 m.
Calculate the work done.

Figure 1 shows a drawer being pulled open.
Calculate the work done.
questions.explanation: Convert to metres first: 80 ÷ 100 = 0.80 m. W = 150 × 0.80 = 120 J. Using 80 directly gives 12 000 J, which is 100 times too big.

questions.question:
A horse pulls a cart with a force of 300 N.
The horse does 2400 J of work.
Calculate the distance the cart moves.
questions.explanation: Rearrange W = F s to s = W ÷ F = 2400 ÷ 300 = 8 m.

questions.question:
A student does 4.5 kJ of work pushing a car a distance of 15 m.
Calculate the force the student applies.
questions.explanation: Convert kilojoules to joules: 4.5 × 1000 = 4500 J. F = W ÷ s = 4500 ÷ 15 = 300 N.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a box being lifted at a steady speed.
Calculate the work done on the box.
gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg
questions.explanation: The lifting force equals the weight, 24.5 N. The distance along the line of action is the height, 1.2 m. W = 24.5 × 1.2 = 29.4 J.

questions.question:
The brakes of a car exert a constant force of 6000 N.
The car travels 35 m while braking.
Calculate the work done by the brakes.
questions.explanation: W = F s = 6000 × 35 = 210 000 J. This energy is transferred from the car's kinetic store to the thermal store of the brakes.

questions.question:
A shopper does 540 J of work pushing a trolley a distance of 450 cm.
Calculate the force the shopper applies.

The crane does 35 280 J of work on the load.
Calculate the height, h, through which the load is lifted.
gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg
questions.explanation: The lifting force equals the weight: 600 × 9.8 = 5880 N. Then s = W ÷ F = 35 280 ÷ 5880 = 6.0 m.

questions.question: What is meant by work done?
acceptedAnswers: force moves object through a distance
markScheme: 1 mark: work is done when a force causes an object to move through a distance (accept energy transferred by a force)
questions.explanation: Work done is the energy transferred when a force moves an object.

questions.question:
Write down the equation that links work done, force and distance.
Give the unit of work done.
markScheme: 1 mark: work done = force × distance (W = Fs)
questions.explanation: W = F s is a recall equation; work done is measured in joules.

questions.question: Define one joule in terms of force and distance.
markScheme: 1 mark: work done when a force of 1 newton
1 mark: causes a displacement of 1 metre (in the direction of the force)
questions.explanation: This definition is why 1 J = 1 N m.

questions.question: A cyclist brakes hard to stop. Explain why the brake pads become hot.
markScheme: 1 mark: friction between the brake pads and the wheel/disc does work
1 mark: energy is transferred from the kinetic energy store of the bike (and cyclist)
1 mark: to the thermal energy store of the brake pads, so their temperature rises
questions.explanation: Braking is work done against friction. The work done transfers the bike's kinetic energy to the thermal store of the brakes.

questions.question: A person pushes a heavy shopping trolley along a flat floor at a steady speed. Describe the energy transfer involved.
markScheme: 1 mark: energy transferred from the chemical energy store of the person (by work done by the push)
1 mark: to the thermal energy store of the trolley wheels / floor / surroundings (work done against friction)
questions.explanation: At steady speed the trolley's kinetic store does not change, so the work done by the person is transferred to thermal energy through friction.

questions.question:
On a cold day, a girl rubs her hands together to warm them.
Explain, in terms of work done, why her hands get warmer.
markScheme: 1 mark: a force is applied and the hands move a distance against friction
1 mark: so work is done (against friction)
1 mark: energy is transferred to the thermal energy store of the hands, increasing their temperature
questions.explanation: Moving surfaces against friction means a force acts through a distance, so work is done and the thermal store of the hands increases.

questions.question:
A weightlifter holds a heavy bar still above his head for 3 seconds.
Explain why the weightlifter does no work on the bar during this time.
markScheme: 1 mark: the bar does not move / there is no displacement
1 mark: so W = F × s = F × 0 = 0
questions.explanation: He exerts a large force, and his muscles get tired, but the bar does not move, so the work done on the bar is zero.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows some equipment a student could use to pull a wooden block across a bench at a steady speed.
Describe how the student could measure the work done in pulling the block across the bench.
markScheme: Attach a newtonmeter to the block.
Pull the block horizontally at a steady speed so the reading is constant.
Read the force from the newtonmeter (in N).
Mark a start and finish point; measure the distance moved with a metre rule (in m).
Convert distance to metres if measured in cm.
Calculate work done using W = F × s.
Repeat and take a mean to improve accuracy.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear method measuring force and distance, with W = Fs used to calculate work done.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant steps, e.g. use a newtonmeter or measure distance.
questions.explanation: Work done needs two measurements: the force (newtonmeter) and the distance moved along the line of the force (metre rule). Then W = F s.

questions.question:
A car of mass 1200 kg is travelling along a level road when the driver brakes.
The brakes exert a constant force of 6000 N and the car stops in 35 m.
Explain the energy transfers that take place as the car stops, in terms of work done.
Include a calculation of the work done by the brakes.
markScheme: The brakes apply a frictional force opposing the motion.
The force acts over a distance, so work is done (by friction / against the car's motion).
Energy is transferred from the kinetic energy store of the car.
The kinetic energy store decreases to zero as the car stops.
Energy is transferred to the thermal energy store of the brakes (pads and discs), raising their temperature.
Energy is then dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings (air), and a little by sound.
The work done equals the energy transferred, so about 210 kJ is transferred from the kinetic store.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct calculation with unit, plus a clear, linked explanation of work done by friction and the transfer from kinetic to thermal stores with temperature rise.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct calculation or a good explanation of the energy transfer, with some links.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. brakes get hot, or a partly correct calculation.
questions.explanation: Braking is work done by friction. W = F s = 210 000 J, which is the energy transferred from the car's kinetic store to the thermal store of the brakes and then the surroundings.
